newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia oil workers see strike from Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: Colombia oil workers see strike from Wednesday.

text.p: BOGOTA, April 28 Reuter - Colombia's main oil workers' union will launch an all-out strike from Wednesday if the government does not give ground over key demands, its leaders said Monday.

Antonio Urdinola, head of the state-run oil company Ecopetrol, said there were "profound differences" between the company and the union but said contingency plans had been prepared to guarantee adequate fuel supplies if the stoppage went ahead.

Spokesmen for two of the main foreign multinationals operating in Colombia, Occidental Petroleum Corp and British Petroleum Co Plc , said their production would not be affected by a potential strike but said pumping operations could be hit.

"We hope the government will change its negotiating position but if it maintains its current line then there is no chance of a solution. We guarantee the total paralysis of oil production, refining, distribution and transport," Hernando Hernandez, leader of the 7,000-strong USO oil workers union told Reuters.
The union will hold an extraordinary assembly in the oil production center of Barrancabermeja this evening to ratify the strike call, Hernandez said.
Ecopetrol and the USO union have been bogged down in collective contract negotiations since early January.

The main sticking points are the USO's demands that Ecopetrol should not be split into separate organizations for crude and gas production, which it believes could be a half-way house on the road to possible privatization.
The union is also calling for more workers to be taken on for the number of sub-contracted workers to be scaled back.
The third main bone of contention is the continuing dispute over the arrest of a number of union members, late last year, on charges of dynamiting oil pipelines.

"There are two types of differences still over economic policy and the legal charges facing USO members...on the issue of labor there's also a very profound difference," Urdinola told the Caracol radio network.

He said the bill to divide the operations of Ecopetrol was currently being considered by Congress and said the charges facing a handful of union members was a question for the legal authorities. Urdinola said contingency plans had been laid which would ensure oil supplies for "many days".
The plan would see non-unionized Ecopetrol workers and officials running plants and key installations although USO members would try to prevent this by setting up pickets, Hernandez said.
Urdinola said it would seek to any strike declared illegal immediately but Hernandez vowed such a move would not halt the oil workers' protest.

"In the event of a strike there could be a problem with pumping because Ecopetrol, is responsible for that...but a strike does not mean our production or exports would stop because we have stocks in storage," a BP spokesman said.
